item.title: bicep-deploy vs bicep-action: A Tool or a Workflow?
item.description:
Azure/bicep-deploy vs bicep-action: A Tool or a Workflow?

I maintain innofactororg/bicep-action, so I should say up front that I am not a neutral party. I am also the person who most needs this comparison to be honest, because every time someone evaluates bicep-action for a new estate, the first question is the obvious one: why not just use Microsoft’s?

item.title: Letting AI operate production Azure — what it gets wrong
item.description:
Abstract

Real failure stories from AI-assisted operations, each with the guardrail that fixed it:

  • an Azure GET can’t prove a property is settable (recommended four times off an empty read);
  • advising a change from a stale read in the middle of a cutover;
  • restating a verified fact until it’s wrong;
  • a disk caching change that hot-detached a production disk;
  • “a freeze is not a control”.

Plus the patterns that worked: subagents, cross-model review with gh copilot, and grep-verifying every HIGH finding. It’s honest, funny, and very MVP.

item.title: bicep-action: Plan, Review and Deploy Bicep from Pull Requests
item.description: Terraform teams stopped deploying blind years ago. They open a pull request, a bot runs terraform plan and posts the result as a comment, a colleague reads exactly what will be created, changed and destroyed, and only then does anyone type atlantis apply. Most Bicep teams still merge and find out. The pipeline runs, the deployment succeeds or fails, and the first time anyone sees what Azure actually did is in the activity log afterwards.

item.title: Terraform or Bicep for Azure: Strengths Compared
item.description:
Considering Terraform and Bicep

As more organizations adopt cloud infrastructure, the demand for infrastructure as code (IAC) solutions has grown. Infrastructure as code allows developers to manage and automate infrastructure deployments using code, making it easier to track changes and maintain consistency.

Terraform and Bicep are two popular IAC solutions that enable developers to manage and automate infrastructure deployments using code.

item.title: Getting Azure Function Keys with ARM Templates
item.description:
Today’s conundrum: I’ve deployed a new Function Application, and another service needs a key to call it. API Management is a good example. The infrastructure deployment should prepare that integration without someone opening the portal, copying a key and pasting it into the next configuration step.

ARM templates can create a named host key and retrieve its value through listKeys. Giving the integration its own named key also makes its purpose clearer than reusing a generic default key.

The examples below show the resource definition and the lookup used in my original deployment. They are fragments to merge into an existing Function App template, not a complete deployment on their own.

item.title: Azure Tags as Bicep Parameters
item.description:
A deployment often needs to find infrastructure that already exists. A virtual machine might belong to a subscription with a shared Recovery Services vault, while its backup policy depends on the workload. Passing the vault name, its resource group and the policy name into every deployment works, but repeats configuration that may already be recorded in Azure.

In the earlier post, Azure Tags as ARM Template Parameters, I used tags to look up those values from an ARM JSON template. This is the same lab scenario expressed in Bicep. The lookup behaves the same way, but the string interpolation makes the resource paths easier to follow.

item.title: Azure Tags as ARM Template Parameters
item.description:
Azure as a State Machine, dogfooding Tags

In the post, I am going to introduce a concept which will allow you to greatly up your Infrastructure as Code game, by using Azure as a State Machine!

One of the typical challenges when deploying ARM templates, is the sheer number of parameters which we find as a requirement to complete a deployment; which as you will appreciate gets considerably harder as we target many environments.

item.title: Appending Tags to Azure Resources with ARM Templates
item.description:
Todays conundrum: As I am leveraging templates, there will always be some standard tags I require to implement within the template, but I also require to provide additional tags as a parameter to be appended with the deployment.

My objective is to set up tags within an ARM template in accordance with good governance and the Cloud adoption framework.

Solution

ARM Template functions to the rescue. Todays salvation is called union, which you can learn more about on the actual [reference site][https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/resource-group-template-functions-array#union]

item.title: Azure Policy as Code: Escaping Quotes in ARM Templates
item.description:
My colleagues and friends Tao Yang , and Stanislav Zhelyazkov have both recently posts interesting topics on how to implement your Azure Policy as Code which I strongly recommend you take a few moments to review

  • Using ARM Templates to deploy azure policy definitions that require input parameters
  • Defining input parameters for policy definitions in ARM Templates

Improving Readability

Both of these topics address the core of the challenges we face when approaching policy as an Infrastructure as Code problem. However, one of the things that is lost in the translation is the readability of the templates which they are deploying.
